items.originalTitle: Much shorter version of GRH Lean verification from Anthropic
items.summary: Anthropic has published a Lean 4 formal proof of the Generalized Riemann Hypothesis (GRH) for Dirichlet L-functions, building on Levent Alpöge's work and using Claude, their AI assistant. The repository includes two editions: a readable version with about 300,000 lines and a compact version with about 76,000 lines, both requiring Lean v4.35.0 and Mathlib for building. The proof has passed machine verification but has not yet been reviewed by mathematicians or accompanied by a formal paper.

items.title: OpenAI corrects GPT-6.2 billing error, increasing Astra usage limits by 40% and Sol by 25%, adds banked reset for affected users [ ~ ] [ ◻ ]
items.originalTitle: OpenAI cuts GPT-6.2 usage: Astra hits limits 40% faster, Sol 25% faster
items.summary: OpenAI acknowledged a billing mistake at the launch of GPT-6.2 that had incorrectly discounted usage for Astra and Sol models, causing users to consume their plan allowances faster than intended. The company fixed the error, resulting in users reaching their limits 40% faster on GPT-6.2 Astra and 25% faster on Sol compared to last week, though these models still offer more usage than previous versions. Other models were unaffected, and OpenAI will not charge users retroactively for the difference. As compensation, OpenAI is providing one banked reset to all users on Go, Plus, Pro, and Business plans.

items.title: Researchers build ASTERISM, a large multi-image benchmark revealing multimodal LLMs often rely on single-image shortcuts, and propose cross-image credit assignment to improve training [ ~ ] [ ◻ ]
items.originalTitle: ASTERISM: Do Multimodal LLMs Actually Look at All the Images?
items.summary:
Researchers audited 33,000 items from 19 public multi-image benchmarks and found that 24.2% can be answered using only one image or the question alone, leading multimodal large language models (MLLMs) to take a single-image shortcut even when multiple images are needed. They created ASTERISM, the largest audited multi-image benchmark with 18,700 items requiring multiple images, along with training and hard subsets. The strongest proprietary MLLM scored 68% on the hardest subset.

The study found that reinforcement learning with verifiable rewards (RLVR), commonly used in MLLM post-training, inadvertently rewards this shortcut because correct answers from one image receive the same reward as those combining multiple images. To address this, the researchers proposed cross-image credit assignment (CICA), an extension of RLVR that shifts credit toward tokens requiring multiple images. Applying CICA to three open-source MLLMs improved ASTERISM scores by 2.6 to 6.0 points, more than doubling gains from other reinforcement learning objectives trained on the same data.

items.originalSummary: arXiv:2611.32316v2 Announce Type: replace-cross Abstract: Multi-image benchmarks aim to test whether a multimodal large language model (MLLM) combines evidence across images, but many of their items can be answered from a single image. Across about 33k items from 19 public benchmarks, our audit and a two-stage single-image filter find that one image or the question alone settles 24.2% of them. On these items, MLLMs recover from one image a median 78% of the accuracy that all images add over the text alone, so these items reward answering from one image, which we call the single-image shortcut. MLLMs take this shortcut even on items where one image is not enough. On such items, most of their wrong answers repeat an answer they give from one image, at a rate well above chance. We build ASTERISM, to our knowledge the largest audited multi-image benchmark, from these 19 benchmarks by keeping their items that need more than one image. Its 18.7k items, 2.0k of them corrected or rewritten, share one format, one scorer and seven task categories. We also release ASTERISM-Train with 49k training items and ASTERISM-Lite, a hard subset whose items we manually verify one by one. On ASTERISM-Lite, the strongest proprietary MLLM scores 68%. Reinforcement learning with verifiable rewards (RLVR), now common in MLLM post-training, rewards the shortcut as well, because a correct answer read off one image earns as much reward as one that combines images. In line with this, existing RLVR objectives add little to the ASTERISM score. To stop rewarding the shortcut in training as ASTERISM does in evaluation, we propose cross-image credit assignment (CICA), an extension of RLVR that moves the credit toward the tokens that need more than one image. On three open-source MLLMs, CICA raises the ASTERISM score by 2.6 to 6.0 points, more than twice the gain of each general and vision-specific RL objective trained on the same data.

items.title: Researchers introduce Actionwave, a benchmark for waveform-centric clinical prediction across ICU, operating room, and emergency settings, comparing models on 20 tasks with 1.4 million labeled windows [ ~ ] [ ◻ ]
items.originalTitle: Actionwave: A Systematic Benchmark for Waveform-Centric Clinical Prediction Across Care Scenarios
items.summary:
Actionwave is a new benchmark designed to evaluate clinical prediction models that use continuous bedside waveform data across intensive care, operating room, and emergency department scenarios. It standardizes prediction tasks by decision time and clinical inference goals, varying conditions such as warning time before interventions to reflect real clinical use. The benchmark compares diverse model architectures and pretrained biosignal encoders under fixed model size and compute constraints, using patient-level data splits and strict information cutoffs to isolate modeling factors.

The study includes over 87,000 model fits across 20 tasks derived from source datasets totaling 1.4 million labeled windows. Results highlight the importance of task-specific model choices and demonstrate why matched cohorts, unimodal controls, and explicit timing are critical for interpreting waveform model performance in clinical prediction.

items.originalSummary: arXiv:2611.31249v2 Announce Type: replace Abstract: Continuous bedside waveforms record rapid physiological changes that can inform clinical decisions. Existing benchmarks examine selected prediction conditions, but it remains unclear how model advantages depend on signal duration, warning time, and available inputs across care settings. We introduce Actionwave, a benchmark for waveform-centric clinical prediction across intensive-care, operating-room, and emergency-department settings. Actionwave uses a common decision-time prediction interface and groups clinically grounded tasks by what is inferred and when. It varies conditions relevant to clinical use, including the warning required before an intervention. We compare diverse architectures and pretrained biosignal encoders under specified model-size and compute budgets. The protocol requires patient-level splits, strict information cutoffs, and comparisons that isolate individual modeling factors. Across 20 tasks and 1.4M task-labelled windows from source datasets, the experimental grids account for over 87,000 model fits. These comparisons identify task-specific choices and show why matched cohorts, unimodal controls, and explicit timing are necessary when interpreting waveform model performance.

items.title: LEGOSpec framework decomposes and optimizes speculative draft models for large language model acceleration, improving acceptance length by up to 34.7% on long-context workloads [ ~ ] [ ◼ ]
items.originalTitle: LEGOSpec: A Composable and Efficient Framework for Speculative Draft Design and Training
items.summary:
LEGOSpec is a composable framework designed to improve speculative decoding in large language models by breaking down draft models into Context, Backbone, Proposal, and Objective components within a unified training system. The framework systematically evaluates component effects and interactions, revealing that different workloads benefit from tailored backbones, proposal designs must balance acceptance and latency, and training objectives should optimize token distribution matching and acceptance length.

Using these insights, the authors developed DFlux, a general-purpose draft model combining a hybrid backbone, residual corrector, and hierarchical supervision, which outperforms previous baselines by up to 13.7% on standard benchmarks and 34.7% on long-context tasks across Qwen and Gemma models. LEGOSpec also enhances training efficiency through metadata-aware scheduling and asynchronous execution, boosting throughput by up to 79% and speeding offline supervision preparation by over three times compared to prior methods.

items.originalSummary: arXiv:2611.33004v2 Announce Type: replace Abstract: Speculative decoding accelerates large language model (LLM) generation using a lightweight draft. Existing methods evaluate complete recipes under different training configurations, leaving component effects, interactions, and composition benefits unclear. Therefore, we present LEGOSpec, a composable framework for speculative draft design and training. LEGOSpec decomposes draft models into Context, Backbone, Proposal, and Objective components that share a unified training infrastructure. Using LEGOSpec, we systematically vary components and evaluate selected combinations under matched training conditions to isolate their effects and interactions. These experiments reveal three findings: (1) Different workloads favor different backbones, depending on context length and memory budget, with within-block dependency modeling particularly important for long contexts. (2) Proposal design must balance acceptance and latency. (3) The training objective should match token distributions locally and optimize acceptance length across the block. These findings guide workload-aware configurations and DFlux, a balanced general-purpose draft combining a convolution-equipped SWA--GQA hybrid backbone, Residual Corrector, and hierarchical supervision. Across Qwen and Gemma models, DFlux improves acceptance length over the strongest baseline by up to 13.7% on regular benchmarks and 34.7% on long-context workloads. To support efficient training, LEGOSpec integrates metadata-aware scheduling and asynchronous execution, increasing training throughput by up to 79% and accelerating offline supervision preparation by up to $3.11\times$ over SpecForge.

items.title: Researchers introduce OmniAct, a cross-embodiment manipulation policy trained on one million robot designs to adapt behavior to diverse robot kinematics and achieve high task success [ ~ ] [ ◼ ]
items.originalTitle: OmniAct: One Policy, One Million Embodiments
items.summary: OmniAct is a manipulation policy that conditions on each robot's kinematic graph to produce embodiment-specific behavior, enabling control across robots with varying degrees of freedom and configurations. The researchers procedurally generated and filtered one million physically feasible robot embodiments, developed algorithms to simulate trajectories for all, and trained OmniAct on diverse manipulation tasks. In evaluations on 2,000 held-out embodiment-scene pairs, OmniAct achieved a 63.0% success rate, outperforming baselines and showing nearly double the success on a previously unseen real-world robot compared to the next best method. The policy learns distinct manipulation strategies that leverage each robot's unique morphology and capabilities.

items.originalSummary: arXiv:2611.33158v2 Announce Type: replace-cross Abstract: A single policy that controls diverse robots must not only transfer task knowledge across embodiments, but also adapt its behavior to each robot's capabilities. Existing approaches facilitate transfer through shared action representations, but these representations do not necessarily capture how differences in robot morphology should shape manipulation strategies. We introduce OmniAct, a cross-embodiment manipulation policy that conditions directly on each robot's kinematics in a specific scene to produce embodiment-specific behavior. This kinematic graph represents the robot's joint positions, motion axes, and connectivity to its visual observation, allowing the policy to account for how its embodiment related to objects and surfaces in the scene. A flow-matching policy predicts relative joint motions for each node, enabling control across robots with different degrees of freedom and kinematic configurations. To learn how physical structure shapes behavior at scale, we procedurally design and filter one million physically feasible robot embodiments; next, we develop algorithms to generate robot trajectories in simulation for all embodiments; finally, we train across diverse simulated manipulation tasks. On 2,000 embodiment-scene-held-out evaluation episodes, OmniAct achieves 63.0% success, compared to 17.8% for pi 0.5 and 57.9% for the strongest baseline; on the task families GPT-6 Astra was evaluated on, it achieves 64.7% against GPT-6 Astra's 41.1%. On a previously unseen real-world robot, it achieves nearly twice the success rate of the next best method, MolmoAct2. Beyond task success, we observe that OmniAct learns distinct manipulation strategies that exploit the capabilities and accommodate the limitations of different morphologies. Project: https://omniact.github.io/

items.title: Researchers introduce CogLoadBench to measure extraneous cognitive load effects on large language models across reasoning tasks and propose Extraneous Load Score to estimate and mitigate load impact [ ~ ] [ ◻ ]
items.originalTitle: Extraneous Cognitive Load in Large Language Models
items.summary: Researchers have developed CogLoadBench, a benchmark designed to isolate and measure extraneous cognitive load effects on large language models (LLMs) by varying presentation factors across reasoning tasks. They found that higher extraneous load often reduces model accuracy by increasing competition or complicating reasoning paths. To address this, they propose the Extraneous Load Score (ELS), a metric computed from model activations that estimates extraneous load and generalizes across tasks and load levels. The study also demonstrates that adjusting model representations toward lower-load directions during inference can improve performance without altering prompt content.

items.originalSummary: arXiv:2611.33197v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: Cognitive Load Theory (CLT) shows that human problem-solving is affected by both intrinsic load, arising from task difficulty, and extraneous load, arising from how task information is presented. Large language models (LLMs) show analogous effects: presentation alone can affect model performance, but these effects have not yet been systematically isolated from task difficulty. To address this gap, we introduce CogLoadBench, a controlled benchmark that varies five CLT-inspired presentation factors across three reasoning task families. Across models, we find that higher extraneous load conditions often reduce accuracy by either adding competition or complicating the reasoning path. To support diagnosis and mitigation of load-related effects, we propose the Extraneous Load Score (ELS), a prompt-time metric computed from activations that estimates a model's extraneous load, and show that it generalizes across reasoning task types and load levels. We further show that shifting model representations toward lower-load directions at inference time can improve average model performance without changing prompt content.

items.title: Researchers analyze dependency-ready decoding in masked diffusion language models, finding limited benefits beyond left-to-right decoding and questioning reliance on attention mechanisms [ ~ ] [ ◻ ]
items.originalTitle: Pitfalls of Dependency-Ready Decoding for Masked Diffusion Language Models
items.summary: Masked diffusion models (MDMs) have demonstrated strong performance on structured reasoning tasks by allowing flexible token unmasking orders. Researchers examined the principle of dependency-ready decoding, which prioritizes resolving token dependencies before unmasking, to assess its impact on accuracy from both practical and theoretical perspectives. They found that decoders implementing dependency readiness through attention often revert to left-to-right decoding when outperforming confidence-based methods. Theoretical analysis introduced an information-theoretic measure of dependency and showed that when prediction margins are large, maximum-margin decoding already commits to dependency-ready tokens, limiting the scope for future dependency-ready decoders. These findings suggest that the potential advantage of dependency-ready decoding is confined to cases with small margins and that reliance on attention for this purpose should be reconsidered.

items.originalSummary: arXiv:2611.33823v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: Masked diffusion models (MDMs) have shown strong performance on structured reasoning tasks such as Sudoku, Trip Planning, and Countdown. MDMs introduce a freedom in the order in which tokens may be unmasked, and to exercise this freedom for good accuracy, early decoding strategies relied on signals of confidence or the downstream impact of decoding a token. However, simple examples seem to illustrate that resolving a token's dependencies before unmasking it should be important. Therefore, we examine whether this principle, which we call dependency-ready decoding, would contribute to better accuracy, from a practical and a theoretical perspective. We examine a recent decoder that implements dependency-readiness through attention, and generally find that when it performs better than confidence-based or future utility baselines, its decoding order collapses to left-to-right decoding. For theoretical analysis, we establish a definition of dependency without resorting to attention, measured by an information-theoretic score of how much revealing a single masked token (or a set) would shift the model's prediction for another. We prove that when the margin is large relative to this score, no such revelation can change the top prediction, so in this regime Maximum-Margin decoding already commits dependency-ready tokens. These findings leave only a narrow scope for future dependency-ready decoders: their potential benefit is limited to positions with margins smaller than the information-theoretic sensitivity, and reliance on attention should be questioned.

items.title: Researchers present closed-form weight-space programming using LLM-written classifiers on a frozen RoBERTa-large encoder, matching or exceeding gradient fine-tuning on multiple datasets without updating encoder weights [ ~ ] [ ◻ ]
items.originalTitle: Fine-Tuning Without Gradients? Closed-Form, LLM-Written Classifiers on a Frozen Encoder
items.summary: Researchers introduce closed-form weight-space programming (WSP), where a large language model writes programs that fit classifiers on a frozen masked language model using cloze-style prompts and closed-form methods, avoiding gradient computation and encoder updates. Evaluated on RoBERTa-large across 11 development datasets with 512 to 8,192 labels, WSP outperforms full fine-tuning and LoRA at all label budgets and approaches prompt-based fine-tuning performance, especially excelling in low-label regimes. On six held-out datasets, WSP remains competitive, consistently outperforming LoRA and staying close to full fine-tuning, though prompt-based fine-tuning leads with large label counts. The method is deterministic, requires multiple encoder passes per template, and the study reports extensive experimental details including unsuccessful approaches.

items.originalSummary: arXiv:2611.33972v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: Can a classifier computed in closed form on a frozen encoder match gradient fine-tuning? We present closed-form weight-space programming (WSP): a large language model (LLM), used as a design assistant, writes programs that read a frozen masked language model through cloze-style prompt templates at several layers, fit closed-form heads (shrinkage discriminant analysis, kernel ridge regression and the encoder's label-word prior) on labelled data, and select among a pool of candidate heads by cross-fitting. No gradient is computed and no encoder weight changes. We instantiate the framework on RoBERTa-large. On 11 development datasets with 512 to 8,192 training labels, WSP is ahead of full fine-tuning (FT) and LoRA at every label budget (by 0.3 to 0.6 points on average; the registered non-inferiority tests pass) and within 0.5 points of prompt-based fine-tuning (PFT); these datasets also shaped the recipe. With fewer labels its lead over FT and LoRA grows: 1.2 to 3.5 points with 64 and 128 labels, and 3.8 to 5.3 points in the few-shot setting of 16 labels per class, where WSP is again within half a point of PFT on the development datasets. On six held-out datasets, WSP stays ahead of LoRA and within half a point of FT on average, although with six datasets no registered test passes, and PFT is ahead, by 1.30 points with 8,192 labels. WSP never collapses and is deterministic, but it needs one encoder pass per template (17 here). We report all eight recipe versions, every decision that saw test results, and 27 ideas that did not help.

items.title: Researchers introduce Puzzling-Bench, a benchmark of 23,777 human-written puzzles with community-verified answers from Puzzling Stack Exchange, to evaluate nine language models including GPT-6.1 [ ~ ] [ ◻ ]
items.originalTitle: Puzzling-Bench: Evaluating Language Models on 23,777 Human-Written Puzzles with Community-Verified Answers
items.summary: Puzzling-Bench comprises a diverse set of puzzles such as riddles, ciphers, logic grids, and recreational mathematics, with about one-third including images. Each puzzle includes the author's accepted answer, hints, community tags, and creation dates, enabling detailed analysis and contamination checks against model training data. Nine advanced language models were evaluated using a two-tier scoring system combining exact match and LLM judgment, with GPT-6.1 achieving the highest accuracy of 74.8% on a shared subset of 255 puzzles. A core set of 17 puzzles defeated all models, and an oracle ensemble reached 91% accuracy. A multimodal pilot showed that withholding images reduced model performance significantly. The dataset, scoring pipeline, and provenance data have been publicly released for further research.

items.originalSummary: arXiv:2611.34331v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: We introduce Puzzling-Bench, a benchmark of 23,777 puzzles with community-verified answers drawn from the Puzzling Stack Exchange archive (2014-2026): riddles, ciphers, logic grids, lateral-thinking problems, wordplay and recreational mathematics, a third of them with images. Every puzzle carries the answer accepted by its author, a short reference answer taken from it (LLM-extracted for the evaluation sets and checked on a 50-puzzle human review), the author's own hints, community tags and a creation date, so that the benchmark supports hint ablations, category analysis and a rolling post-cutoff slice (254 puzzles posted after the training cutoff of six of the nine models we evaluate, including the best one) as a contamination check. We evaluate nine frontier and open models with a two-tier scorer (normalized exact match, then an LLM judge) and validate the judge with three judges from two model families: they agree on 95-97% of verdicts (kappa 0.82-0.96), move no model by more than 1.6 points, and show no own-family preference. The best model, GPT-6.1, reaches 74.8% on a shared 255-puzzle set; a hard core of 17 puzzles defeats all nine models; model failures are strongly correlated, and the second-best model contributes a single puzzle to a greedy ensemble, yet an oracle over all nine reaches 91%. On a 100-puzzle multimodal pilot, withholding the question's image costs the two best models 24 and 35 points. We release the dataset, the scoring pipeline and all per-row provenance.

items.originalTitle: Collect for Coverage, Replay with Evidence: Adaptive and Efficient On-Policy Distillation for Long-Horizon Agents
items.summary: CARE-OPD (Collect for coverAge, Replay with Evidence) addresses limitations in fully online on-policy distillation (OPD) for long-horizon agents by expanding history coverage and filtering unreliable updates through student-seeded teacher completions and confidence gating. It also uses hindsight replay allocation to focus on critical decisions during trajectory reuse. Evaluated on long-horizon tasks in software engineering and deep research, CARE-OPD outperforms existing OPD and prefix replay methods, significantly improving task success rates while reducing training time and environment interactions.

items.originalSummary: arXiv:2611.34756v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: Fully online on-policy distillation (OPD) is costly for long-horizon agents because each update depends on fresh environment rollouts. Prefix replay offers an efficient alternative by sampling current-student responses from stored histories, reducing idle time for long-tail rollouts and allowing each collected trajectory to support multiple updates. However, our analysis of the complete prefix replay pipeline identifies two limitations in long-horizon settings. In trajectory collection, teacher-only trajectories miss student-induced histories, while broader history coverage can reduce teacher reliability. In trajectory reuse, fixed position-based schedules cannot identify critical decisions that may occur at any trajectory depth. We introduce CARE-OPD (Collect for coverAge, Replay with Evidence) to address both limitations. Student-seeded teacher completions and response-level confidence gating expand history coverage while filtering unreliable updates. Hindsight replay allocation then uses downstream execution evidence to select consequential turns. Across long-horizon tasks Software Engineering and Deep Research, CARE-OPD outperforms online OPD and prior prefix replay baselines. On SWE-bench Verified, it raises task success to 59.5% while reducing end-to-end training time by 45% and environment actions by 44% relative to asynchronous online OPD.

items.title: PersonaFactory generates over 740,000 synthetic user personas and 1.24 million persona-styled conversations in 85 languages to augment AI training prompts with stylistic diversity [ ~ ] [ ◻ ]
items.originalTitle: PersonaFactory: Stylistic User Prompt Augmentation with Synthetic Persona Bank
items.summary:
PersonaFactory is an end-to-end pipeline that creates detailed synthetic user personas to augment existing user prompts, addressing the lack of stylistic variation in out-of-the-box large language model outputs. It produces a large bank of structured personas and a corpus of persona-styled conversations, enabling more natural and diverse user-AI interactions across multiple languages.

The system uses attribute-based style representations to control style adoption and preserve user intent better than free-text persona descriptions, as evaluated by automated metrics and human experts. PersonaFactory's augmented conversations perform comparably to original training data on capability benchmarks and adapt reply styles more closely to users without explicit steering, improving assistant persona control in AI training.

items.originalSummary: arXiv:2611.34785v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: Large language models increasingly replace real people in the AI development pipeline, as they are used to generate training dialogues at scale and to drive alignment and evaluation. However, out-of-the-box models produce monolingual and stylistically flat texts as synthetic user prompts, failing to replicate the real user-AI communication mechanics. We present PersonaFactory, an end-to-end pipeline that generates detailed user personas and uses them to augment existing user prompts from their point of view, producing a bank of over 740000 structured synthetic personas detailing their background and communication behaviors, and a corpus of roughly 1.24 million persona-styled synthetic conversations spanning 85 languages. We evaluate the effect of personal features on style adoption and intent preservation, using an LLM-judge and heuristic metrics to assess augmentation fidelity together with the downstream impact on assistant persona control through training data. Results show that our structured, attribute-based style representation enables per-axis control and better intent preservation at comparable style fidelity than free-text persona descriptions used in existing methods. A human expert evaluation found the augmented conversations plausible, with favorable ratings for intent preservation, style naturalness, and multilingual authenticity. Finally, PersonaFactory conversations achieve comparable performance to original training data on capability benchmarks, are preferred on real user prompts at equal reply length, and adapt their reply style more closely to users without explicit steering.

items.title: Researchers propose DART method to generate diverse alternative reasoning traces for hard math problems, improving problem recovery by 37% over Monte Carlo sampling [ ~ ] [ ◼ ]
items.originalTitle: Diverse Alternative Reasoning Traces for Hard Math Problems
items.summary:
Researchers introduce Diverse Alternative Reasoning Traces (DART), a method that starts from rejected reasoning traces in large language models and generates distinct alternative reasoning steps to solve difficult math problems. DART ranks uncertain reasoning steps and produces alternative candidates guided by reference answers and meta-thoughts, enhancing problem-solving coverage.

On the DeepMath-103K dataset, DART recovers 37% more problems than independent Monte Carlo sampling at the same number of generated traces, with a 30% lower cost per accepted trace. Post-training the Llama-3.1-8B-Instruct model on DART-mined traces yields top performance in five out of six evaluations on MATH-500 and AIME benchmarks, demonstrating DART's effectiveness in expanding problem coverage and improving training data quality for mathematical reasoning tasks.

items.originalSummary: arXiv:2611.34928v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: Post-training large language models (LLMs) for mathematical reasoning often relies on accepted traces whose final answers pass a verifier. For hard math problems, however, such traces can be rare under independent Monte Carlo (MC) sampling. To address this, we propose Diverse Alternative Reasoning Traces (DART), a trace-mining method that starts from a rejected trace, decomposes it into reasoning steps, and ranks them by position-weighted uncertainty. It then generates deliberately distinct alternative candidates for highly ranked steps using reference-answer guidance and a meta-thought before completing the resulting traces. On greedy-unsolved DeepMath-103K problems, DART recovers 37% more problems than MC sampling at a matched number of generated traces. Its estimated generation cost per recovered problem is nearly identical, while its cost per accepted trace is 30% lower. Post-training Llama-3.1-8B-Instruct on traces mined by DART achieves the highest point estimate in five of six evaluations across MATH-500 and AIME benchmarks. These results demonstrate that revisiting rejected traces with DART can expand problem coverage and provide effective post-training data.

items.title: Researchers find semantic density metrics do not predict memory collapse in LLM agents across multiple task environments
items.originalTitle: Semantic Density Does Not Predict Agent-Memory Collapse
items.summary: Researchers evaluated 14 memory-store statistics, including mean pairwise cosine similarity, across 805 snapshots from 13 memory methods in various task environments to determine if these metrics could warn of declining task accuracy in large language model (LLM) agents. They found no statistic reliably predicted early accuracy decline, with global semantic density measures failing to provide warnings and local crowding metrics not transferring consistently across memory designs. Classifiers trained on this data falsely flagged many stable checkpoints and missed most accuracy drops in extended task runs. The study also observed that size-limited memory stores remained stable over long horizons, while failures occurred only when unbounded whole-store prompting exceeded model input capacity, which was directly predicted by token growth.

items.originalSummary: arXiv:2611.33184v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: Persistent textual memory can improve LLM agents, but repeated updates can erode task performance. We ask whether memory-store statistics warn before held-out accuracy declines. We registered mean pairwise cosine similarity ($\rho$) and 13 additional geometry, retrieval, and graph statistics on 805 snapshots from 13 memory methods across ALFWorld, AppWorld, ScienceWorld, WebShop, and two ARC-AGI settings. These methods store trajectories, rules, workflows, strategies, or linked records, using selective retrieval or whole-store prompting. No such statistic reliably predicted early signs of task accuracy decline, and $\rho$ had zero median lead. With the checkpoint after peak accuracy as a secondary decline point, measures of highly similar pairs and nearest-neighbor crowding changed earlier but did not consistently outperform stored-item count. We trained classifiers on this corpus and applied them unchanged to PropWorld runs of up to 5,000 crafting tasks. They falsely flagged 56.9% of checkpoints from size-limited stores with stable accuracy and detected only 18% of checkpoints after task success fell to zero. Thus, global semantic density did not provide a reliable warning, while local crowding did not transfer consistently across memory designs. In these long-horizon runs, size-limited stores remained stable, while the sole failure arose when unbounded whole-store prompting exceeded model input capacity, which token growth predicted directly.

items.title: Researchers develop supervised learning confidence scores to improve gating of large language model automation, outperforming baselines on a 2B-parameter model [ ~ ] [ ◼ ]
items.originalTitle: Confidence scores for gated automation of large language models
items.summary:
Researchers propose a supervised learning approach to generate reliable confidence scores for large language model (LLM) outputs, addressing the challenge of LLMs producing incorrect answers with high confidence. Their method fits a linear confidence score head to the final-layer hidden state of a frozen 2B-parameter LLM backbone and trains text-only metamodels for closed models, enabling automated confident responses and routing uncertain answers for human review.

The approach was evaluated on datasets primarily from SQuAD and TruthfulQA, outperforming multiple baselines and metamodels by automating the largest fraction of workload at high accuracy targets. While prompted confidence scores may appear calibrated, they often lack the resolution needed for effective thresholding. The confidence score head showed modest transferability to unseen datasets but remained the most robust method. This framework aims to enhance the safety of automating LLM-based agents and can be adapted to gate other properties such as safety or compliance.

items.originalSummary: arXiv:2611.33394v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: AI agents built on large language models (LLMs) demonstrate strong capabilities in automated decision-making. However, LLMs may produce incorrect answers with high confidence, limiting their applicability in decisions that affect individuals and organizations. Reliable confidence scores are necessary to gate such decisions, and existing estimates are frequently unavailable or too coarse to support effective gating. This work uses supervised learning to train models to predict the correctness of LLM-generated answers, enabling automated confident responses and routing uncertain ones for human review. A linear confidence score head is fitted to the final-layer hidden state of the frozen LLM backbone, and text-only metamodels are trained as an alternative for closed models. All results come from a single 2B-parameter backbone, on graded answers that are about 98% SQuAD and the remainder TruthfulQA. Against multiple baselines, the confidence score head outperforms all baselines and metamodels, automating the largest fraction of the workload at high accuracy targets. Prompted confidence scores can appear well calibrated yet lack the resolution needed for thresholding. Although transferability to unseen datasets is modest, the confidence score head remains the most robust approach. The proposed confidence scoring framework enhances the safety of automating LLM-based agents and can be adapted to gate other properties, including safety or compliance.

items.title: Researchers introduce HumblePRM to improve Vision Language Models' abstention in ambiguous cases by independently scoring perception and calibration stages [ ~ ] [ ◼ ]
items.originalTitle: HumblePRM: Improving VLM Abstention in Ambiguous Situations through Process Reward Modeling
items.summary:
Researchers propose HumblePRM, a lightweight process reward model that enhances Vision Language Models' (VLMs) ability to abstain from confident answers when visual evidence is ambiguous. Unlike standard outcome reward models that only supervise final decisions, HumblePRM separately evaluates the perception stage, where the model describes the scene, and the calibration stage, where it judges if the evidence suffices for a conclusion, rewarding alignment between evidence and expressed confidence.

Training with HumblePRM significantly increases abstention on ambiguous inputs without reducing accuracy on clear images, and the improvement also transfers to Gemma 4 E4B, a larger edge model. This approach suggests that process reward supervision can lead to more reliable VLMs with better-calibrated confidence and reduced unpredictable behavior.

items.originalSummary: arXiv:2611.33452v1 Announce Type: cross Abstract: Reliable deployment of Vision Language Models (VLMs) requires that a model's expressed confidence remain grounded in what it can actually see, and that it recognize when the visual evidence is too ambiguous to commit to a confident response. Standard post-training uses outcome reward models (ORMs) that supervise only the final decision, rewarding a confident answer regardless of whether the image supports one, while existing methods either tend to detect uncertainty post-hoc or assume an objective verdict always exists. We instead split multimodal reasoning into two stages: perception, where the model must factually describe the scene, and calibration, where it must judge whether that evidence is sufficient to commit to a conclusion. We introduce HumblePRM, a lightweight process reward model (PRM) that scores each stage independently, rewarding agreement between evidence and expressed confidence rather than outcome correctness alone. Training with HumblePRM increases abstention due to uncertainty on ambiguous inputs considerably while leaving accuracy on clear images roughly unchanged. We also find that the improvement transfers to Gemma 4 E4B, a larger, popular edge model. Our findings show that process reward supervision is a promising route to VLMs with better calibrated abstention, ensuring more reliability rather than unpredictable behavior.

items.title: Researchers present vSFT framework to verbally fine-tune language model agents at test time, improving success rates on ALFWorld and WebShop tasks [ ~ ] [ ◻ ]
items.originalTitle: vSFT: Learning to Verbally Tune Agents at Test Time
items.summary:
Researchers introduce verbally Supervised Fine-Tuning (vSFT), a framework that enables large language model agents to receive dense natural language feedback and update their weights during test time. The system forms a closed loop where a supervisor generates verbal guidance from failed agent trajectories, and a hypernetwork converts this into low-rank weight updates to tune the agent.

The vSFT approach using the Qwen3-4B model outperforms existing reinforcement learning methods like GRPO and Reflexion by significant margins in success rates on ALFWorld and WebShop benchmarks. This method suggests a promising direction for creating agents that can adapt and improve themselves dynamically rather than relying solely on pre-adapted models.

items.originalSummary: arXiv:2611.34440v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: Large language model agents are increasingly improved via agentic reinforcement learning, which can be on-policy but suffers from expensive rollouts and sparse rewards, limiting its application at test time. In this paper, we present a verbally Supervised Fine-Tuning (vSFT) framework that enables the conjunction of dense feedback in natural language and weight updates at test time. Specifically, our vSFT forms a closed loop between an agent and a supervisor via a hypernetwork, in which the supervisor generates verbal supervision from the agent's failed trajectories, and the hypernetwork converts that supervision into low-rank weight updates to tune the agent. We validate that this test-time in-parameter evolving process outperforms both its in-context counterparts and prevalent reinforcement learning methods. In particular, our vSFT using Qwen3-4B outperforms GRPO and Reflexion by 8.7% and 13.9% in success rate on ALFWorld, and by 4.8% and 18.2% on WebShop, respectively. We believe that learning how to adapt a model, rather than an adapted model, offers a promising path towards more capable agents that improve themselves.

items.title: Researchers propose mismatch-corrected bandits to improve adaptive data sampling by modeling proxy-target model discrepancies, reducing training regret and enhancing worst-group accuracy [ ~ ] [ ◼ ]
items.originalTitle: When the Proxy Is Wrong: Mismatch-Corrected Bandits for Adaptive Data Sampling
items.summary:
Researchers address the problem of proxy models ranking training data differently from target models, which can degrade training performance. They model the mismatch between proxy and target models as a multi-fidelity bandit problem, using rare audits to correct proxy rewards and guide data allocation decisions more effectively. The approach audits uncertain decisions and distributes the audit budget over training to minimize regret.

Theoretical analysis proves that proxy-only allocation can lead to linear regret and that a minimum number of paired audits is necessary, with a sliding-window policy achieving improved regret bounds under changing conditions. Experiments on the CivilComments-WILDS dataset demonstrate that mismatch correction improves worst-group accuracy by 6.3 to 10.5 percentage points compared to target-only policies with the same audit budget, validating the method's practical benefits.

items.originalSummary: arXiv:2611.34707v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: Data allocation methods often use a small proxy model to select training data for a larger target model. However, this proxy can rank data differently from the target, leading to suboptimal training performance. To address this problem, we model the mismatch between the proxy and target models and incorporate it into the allocation decision. To do so, the problem is cast as a multi-fidelity bandit, where each arm is a data intervention. The proxy reward is observed every round, whereas the target reward is revealed only on rare audits of the same update. These paired observations identify arm-wise mismatches without assuming a shared offset or preservation of rankings. Mismatch-corrected bandits correct the proxy with paired residuals, audit only uncertain decisions, and pace the audit budget over training. From a theoretical viewpoint, we prove a regret decomposition and lower bounds under stationarity. These bounds show that proxy-only allocation can incur linear regret and that a minimum number of paired audits is necessary. Under abrupt changes, using the audit budget early can also incur linear regret. A sliding-window policy that spreads audits over training achieves regret of order $\sqrt{\Gamma_T T\log T}$ where $\Gamma_T$ denotes the number of change points. Experimentally, we test the approach in a closed-loop proof of concept on CivilComments-WILDS, where BERT-Small guides the training of BERT-Large. Mismatch correction improves worst-group accuracy over a target-only policy with the same target-model budget. Spreading audits over training improves worst-group accuracy by 6.3 to 10.5 percentage points at the same audit count.

items.originalTitle: From Shared Patterns to Individual Evidence: Two-Stage Reasoning for Emerging Entities in Temporal Knowledge Graphs
items.summary:
Researchers introduce INSPIRE, a two-stage forecasting framework designed to improve reasoning over emerging entities in temporal knowledge graphs (TKGs), which face challenges due to sparse and bursty interaction histories. INSPIRE combines a shared-pattern predictor with an individual-evidence adapter that integrates textual semantic priors and long-range event statistics to enhance prediction accuracy.

The framework addresses limitations of existing methods by fusing event-updated memory across candidate catalogs and applying coordinated masking techniques. Evaluations on four benchmarks from ICEWS and GDELT datasets show that INSPIRE significantly improves emerging entity mean reciprocal rank (MRR) by up to 88.83% over strong baselines, with further gains from the individual-evidence adapter. The code for INSPIRE is publicly available for further research and application.

items.originalSummary: arXiv:2611.34708v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: Temporal knowledge graphs (TKGs) continually introduce emerging entities whose interaction histories evolve from zero-shot debuts into sparse, bursty few-shot trajectories. However, current paradigms are fragmented: pattern-transfer methods lack catalog-wide event memory, whereas online memory models suffer from endpoint-role asymmetry that degrades unseen-answer ranking. Furthermore, sparse early interactions exhibit both long-range dispersion and local redundancy under skewed distribution. To address these challenges, we propose INSPIRE (Integrating Shared Patterns and Individual Evidence for Reasoning), a two-stage forecasting framework over a known catalog. In Stage I, INSPIRE learns an availability-aware shared-pattern predictor that fuses event-updated memory across the full candidate catalog while applying coordinated query- and catalog-side masking. Subsequently, Stage II freezes this predictor and optimizes a lightweight individual-evidence adapter (EA) combining textual semantic priors with correlation-weighted long-range event statistics under support- and role-balanced co-answer supervision with prior-odds debiasing and soft residual alignment. In addition, we decompose evaluation by endpoint roles and track longitudinal emerging-answer cohorts via query-micro and answer-entity macro metrics. Across four benchmarks based on the ICEWS and GDELT event datasets, INSPIRE improves Emerging MRR by 16.73%-88.83% over the strongest baselines. Relative to paired Stage I predictors, EA further increases Emerging MRR by 8.28%-32.63%, Answer-new MRR by 7.81%-41.24%, and cohort macro MRR by 9.64%-39.94%, gains attributed to semantic priors and candidate-level score competition suppressing mismatched established competitors without zero-support prior shortcuts. The official code is publicly available at https://github.com/KcAcoZhang/INSPIRE.

items.title: Researchers introduce token readout-based scoring system and J-lens methods to improve model diffing for backdoor detection in fine-tuned models [ ~ ] [ ◻ ]
items.originalTitle: Reading Fine-Tuning Diffs Through Lenses: Model Diffing for Backdoor Detection
items.summary:
Researchers present a unified scoring system using token readouts to evaluate weight, activation, and output-based model diffing methods aimed at detecting backdoors introduced during fine-tuning. They enhance existing weight and activation methods by incorporating the J-lens and its refinement, the J++-lens, and test these approaches by comparing backdoored models with their base counterparts. The J++-lens notably improves weight-based detection, ranking backdoor-related tokens among the top ten in most test settings.

The study finds that output and activation-based methods like ADL and Diff Mining can fail if the backdoored model is penalized during fine-tuning for assigning probability to backdoor trigger words on clean inputs, whereas weight-based methods remain robust. Conversely, manipulating hidden units or restricting training to certain layers can obscure backdoors from weight-based methods but not from activation or output-based ones. No single method effectively resists all tested evasion techniques, highlighting the challenges in backdoor detection.

items.originalSummary: arXiv:2611.34758v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: We introduce a common scoring system based on token readouts to evaluate weight, activation and output-based model diffing methods for backdoor detection in fine-tuning processes. We also improve existing weight and activation based methods by incorporating the $J$-lens and its refinement, the $J{+}{+}$-lens. We test our setup in experiments where we compare a backdoored model with the base model from which it was fine-tuned. Our results show that incorporating the $J{+}{+}$-lens improves the weight-based method in all our settings, while the $J$-lens improves its ranks within single layers. The strongest single method is $\Delta W J{+}{+}$, the weight difference decoded through the $J{+}{+}$-lens of the base model, which ranks a token naming the backdoor among its first ten tokens in 11 of our 12 settings. Moreover, we show that output and activation based methods such as ADL and Diff Mining can easily break if the backdoored model is penalised during fine-tuning for giving the backdoor's words probability on clean inputs, whereas the weight-based methods are not affected. Conversely, permuting the hidden units or training only the layers that read the residual stream hides the backdoor from the weight-based methods but not from ADL and Diff Mining. No single method resists both attacks.

items.title: One Model, Many Modes: Evolving System Prompt Ensembles for Creative Generation [ ~ ] [ ◻ ]
items.originalTitle: One Model, Many Modes: Evolving System Prompt Ensembles for Creative Generation
items.summary: arXiv:2611.34760v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: Preference-aligned LLMs can exhibit mode collapse, concentrating their output distributions around a narrow set of high-reward responses. This limits creative generation, which requires quality, novelty, and diversity. Existing test-time methods often emphasize diversity, giving less attention to whether individual responses are both high-quality and novel. This distinction matters in practical use, where users may seek a single compelling, original response. We formalize creative generation as a multi-objective distributional optimization problem and introduce SEPO, a training-free framework for System Prompt Ensemble Optimization. The framework combines prompt evolution with greedy max-min selection to identify behaviorally distinct system prompts under a quality constraint, then uniformly samples one prompt per response at inference time. Across four creative generation tasks with increasing quality requirements and three open-weight models, SEPO ranks first in 8 of 12 settings on the harmonic mean of quality, diversity, and novelty, while no baseline leads in more than two. On average, it raises LLM-judged diversity from 1.92 to 3.43 and novelty from 1.00 to 3.34 over base sampling (1-5 scale), with quality decreasing from 3.72 to 3.30. We further show that expanding the optimized ensemble increases separation among prompt-conditioned response distributions. These results support system prompt ensemble optimization as a promising approach to improving LLM creativity at inference time.

items.title: When Every Rollout Fails: Splicing Learner-Conditioned Options into Long-Horizon Agent RL [ ~ ] [ ◻ ]
items.originalTitle: When Every Rollout Fails: Splicing Learner-Conditioned Options into Long-Horizon Agent RL
items.summary: arXiv:2611.34777v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: Group-based reinforcement learning with verifiable rewards often yields all-fail groups on long-horizon agent tasks: every sampled trajectory receives zero reward, leaving group-relative methods without a reward-based policy gradient. A common remedy supplies complete solutions from a stronger model, but full trajectories are expensive and expose the learner to long off-policy histories. We introduce SPLICE, which constructs local training targets from failed current-policy trajectories online. For each all-fail group, a proposal model selects a splice point in a current-policy trajectory and generates several bounded options from that point. We estimate each option's value using repeated current-policy continuations, convert positive estimates into a return-weighted local target, and fit the current policy on the options. We evaluate SPLICE across two policy families on two long-horizon agent tasks, Software Engineering with SWE-bench Verified and Deep Research with BrowseComp-Plus. SPLICE outperforms GRPO and full-trajectory guidance baselines in all four settings, improving over GRPO by 2.8--9.8 percentage points. On initially failed SWE tasks, it raises GRPO's graduation rate by 10.8 percentage points. Further experiments show that SPLICE improves performance while reducing costly proposal-model computation.

items.title: Explaining Chess and Go with Discovered Motifs [ ~ ] [ ◻ ]
items.originalTitle: Explaining Chess and Go with Discovered Motifs
items.summary: arXiv:2610.23166v2 Announce Type: replace Abstract: Modern chess engines play far beyond human ability, often choosing moves whose underlying ideas are difficult for humans to understand. We propose an automatic metric for chess explanations based on how well the motifs they describe generalize to new positions. Evaluating state-of-the-art language models using this metric, we find that they perform surprisingly poorly, often relying on surface-level board observations rather than robust, transferable chess concepts. We then introduce BinProp, a training-free method that enables these same models to discover reusable chess concepts and use them to explain moves in natural language. BinProp improves motif generalization for every model tested, nearly tripling the average score compared with direct prompting. Beyond chess, the same method discovers useful concepts in Go, draughts, and shogi without additional tuning.

items.title: Where Is Uncertainty Observed? A Mechanistic Understanding of Uncertainty Quantification in LLMs [ ~ ] [ ◻ ]
items.originalTitle: Where Is Uncertainty Observed? A Mechanistic Understanding of Uncertainty Quantification in LLMs
items.summary: arXiv:2611.15735v2 Announce Type: replace Abstract: Knowing when a large language model's (LLM's) response can be trusted is critical for its safe use. Uncertainty quantification (UQ) can help LLMs recognize if their responses may be unreliable. Existing taxonomies organize UQ methods by uncertainty source or estimation mechanism. They leave unresolved the question of where uncertainty is observed in the model's computation. The answer matters because the observation point determines whether an estimator has access to enough information to recover a given target, and how well it can recover it. Drawing on mechanistic interpretability, we define four mechanistic observation lenses: the structural lens observes component updates, the representational lens observes hidden states, the distributional lens observes token probabilities, and the semantical lens observes distributions over meanings. We relate these lenses through the residual stream and order them by the information they carry, which gives a principle for selecting UQ methods for different targets. We survey existing methods through the four lenses. Furthermore, we distinguish evaluation targets, criteria, and metrics to clarify different UQ evaluation protocols. Finally, we identify open problems and research directions to connect uncertainty estimation to the internal computation and downstream use of LLMs.

items.title: Search From the Start: Search-Native Pretraining for Language Models [ ~ ] [ ◼ ]
items.originalTitle: Search From the Start: Search-Native Pretraining for Language Models
items.summary: arXiv:2611.26809v2 Announce Type: replace Abstract: Modern language models (LMs) are increasingly deployed with access to search tools at inference. Yet pretraining remains predominantly focused on predicting static text, with search capabilities typically introduced during post-training. We propose Search-Native Pretraining as a practical route to teach search capability during pretraining from ordinary text corpora. Specifically, we augment pretraining corpus at scale with web-search queries and retrieve web response using a local index. Training on this augmented corpus teaches models to generate search calls and incorporate retrieved evidence during language modeling. Across Wikipedia and DCLM-Edu corpora and 360M to 3.3B parameter scales, search-pretrained models ("QueryLM") show improved performance on knowledge-intensive tasks and higher steerability toward the retrieved evidence. Crucially, their advantage persists after supervised fine-tuning of both search-pretrained and conventionally pretrained models, indicating that the tested post-training procedures do not fully recover the capabilities developed during pretraining. Throughout our experiments, we find that a 1.4B QueryLM consistently beats or matches the performance of a FLOP-matched 3.3B baseline model across all knowledge intensive tasks. These results establish search-pretraining as a practical way to develop foundational search capabilities during pretraining. We release the training artifacts, including model checkpoints and data.

items.title: GDS Agent for Graph Algorithmic Reasoning [ ~ ] [ ◼ ]
items.originalTitle: GDS Agent for Graph Algorithmic Reasoning
items.summary: arXiv:2508.20637v3 Announce Type: replace Abstract: Large language models (LLMs) have shown remarkable multimodal information processing and reasoning ability. When equipped with tools through function calling and enhanced with retrieval-augmented techniques, compound LLM-based systems can access closed data sources and answer questions about them. However, they still struggle to process and reason over large-scale graph-structure data. In this technical report we introduce the GDS (Graph Data Science) agent. The GDS agent introduces a comprehensive set of graph algorithms as tools, together with preprocessing (retrieval) and postprocessing of algorithm results, in a model context protocol (MCP) server. It is accompanied by a skill that guides the LLM through graph analysis. The agent can be used with any modern LLM out-of-the-box. GDS agent allows users to ask any question that implicitly and intrinsically requires graph algorithmic reasoning about their data, and quickly obtain accurate and grounded answers. We introduce new benchmarks that evaluate intermediate tool calls as well as final responses, and the results indicate that the GDS agent solves a wide spectrum of graph tasks. We also demonstrate how the GDS agent can perform open-ended analyses at the level of domain experts, on tasks such as money laundering tracing and pattern mining in biology. Finally, we discuss the remaining challenges and the future roadmap.

items.title: Network of Theseus (like the ship) [ ~ ] [ ◻ ]
items.originalTitle: Network of Theseus (like the ship)
items.summary: arXiv:2512.04198v2 Announce Type: replace Abstract: A standard assumption in deep learning is that the inductive bias introduced by a neural network architecture must persist from training through inference. The architecture you train with is the architecture you deploy. This assumption constrains the community from selecting architectures that may have desirable efficiency or design properties due to difficulties with optimization. We challenge this assumption with the Network of Theseus (NoT), a method for progressively converting a trained, or even untrained, guide network architecture part-by-part into an entirely different target network architecture while preserving the performance of the guide network. At each stage, components in the guide network architecture are incrementally replaced with the target architecture modules and aligned via representational similarity metrics. This procedure preserves most of the functionality of the guide network even under substantial architectural changes-for example, converting a convolutional network into a multilayer perceptron, or GPT-2 into a recurrent neural network. By decoupling optimization from deployment, NoT expands the space of viable inference-time architectures, opening opportunities for better accuracy-efficiency tradeoffs and enabling more directed exploration of the architectural design space.

items.title: Neural Isomorphic Fields: A Transformer-based Algebraic Numerical Embedding [ ~ ] [ ◻ ]
items.originalTitle: Neural Isomorphic Fields: A Transformer-based Algebraic Numerical Embedding
items.summary: arXiv:2601.12095v2 Announce Type: replace Abstract: Neural network models often face challenges when processing very small or very large numbers due to issues such as overflow, underflow, and unstable output variations. To mitigate these problems, we propose using embedding vectors for numbers instead of directly using their raw values. These embeddings aim to retain essential algebraic properties while preventing numerical instabilities. We introduce Neural Isomorphic Fields (NIF), a digit-sequence Transformer autoencoder trained with two learned commutative operators and an antisymmetric neural comparator. At zero loss, the embeddings provably form an ordered integral domain isomorphic to the decimal fractions, whose field of fractions is isomorphic to the rationals. For the trained model, we bound errors of operations, chains and algebraic laws by decoding margins, defects and Lipschitz constants. Trained on up to 25 digits, NIF reaches at least 99.9% exact match on closure, identity, associativity and distributivity and 99.8% on ten-step chains and the order relation. With four channels per decimal place, reconstruction and both operations exceed 99.7% exact match on numbers of up to 200 digits whose parts stay within training lengths, so the dimension grows linearly. In a language model, frozen operators raise exact match on 14-20-digit word problems from 12.0% (operators off) to 39.7%.

items.title: Thinking Deeper, Not Longer: Memory-Efficient Latent Chain-of-Thought with Depth-Recurrent Transformers for Compositional Generalization [ ~ ] [ ◻ ]
items.originalTitle: Thinking Deeper, Not Longer: Memory-Efficient Latent Chain-of-Thought with Depth-Recurrent Transformers for Compositional Generalization
items.summary: arXiv:2603.21676v3 Announce Type: replace Abstract: Standard Transformers have a fixed computational depth, limiting their ability to generalize to tasks that require variable-depth reasoning. The usual remedy, Chain-of-Thought (CoT), spends tokens to reason, inflating the key--value cache, so memory becomes the limiting cost when reasoning is served over large query batches. We study a depth-recurrent Transformer that decouples computational depth from parameter count by iterating a shared-weight block, so that adding reasoning steps leaves peak inference memory unchanged and grows latency only linearly, with no token generation. Three ingredients support the recurrence over 20+ thinking steps: a silent thinking objective that supervises only the final output, LayerScale initialization, and an identity-biased gate that opens a gradient highway across steps. We characterize it on three compositional domains with decreasing structural bias: graph reachability (adjacency masking), nested boolean logic (relative positioning), and unstructured relational text (no structural positional cue). We find a \emph{computational frontier}: accuracy climbs once the thinking-step count meets the task's complexity, reaching near-perfect performance on the two structured tasks and a lower plateau on unstructured text. How it climbs depends on the structural bias---abruptly from chance on the graph task, gradually on the other two. Depth recurrence extrapolates beyond the training range: it succeeds on the graph task where fixed-depth models barely extrapolate, and on the two sequence tasks comes within two points of fixed-depth Transformers that use $4$--$6.4\times$ more parameters. On the graph task, whose adjacency mask makes propagation depth verifiable, intermediate per-step supervision---a standard recipe for deep iterative models---consistently \emph{harms} this extrapolation at widths $d \geq 256$. We release the code for reproducibility.

items.title: NSFL: A Post-Training Neuro-Symbolic Fuzzy Logic Framework for Boolean Operators in Neural Embeddings [ ~ ] [ ◻ ]
items.originalTitle: NSFL: A Post-Training Neuro-Symbolic Fuzzy Logic Framework for Boolean Operators in Neural Embeddings
items.summary: arXiv:2604.10604v2 Announce Type: replace-cross Abstract: Standard dense retrievers have no native mechanism for multi-atom logical constraints. We introduce Neuro-Symbolic Fuzzy Logic (NSFL), a training-free framework that brings fuzzy-logical structure to neural embedding spaces through a first-order finite-difference treatment of similarity. NSFL anchors logical operations on zero-order atomic scores while steering with Neuro-Symbolic Deltas (NS-Delta) -- the marginal semantic contributions induced by contextual fusion -- preserving atomic meaning while capturing contextual dependence, and avoiding the representation collapse and manifold escape endemic to geometric baselines. For latency-constrained deployment, Spherical Query Optimization (SQO) uses Riemannian optimization to project logical formulas into manifold-stable query vectors. Across six encoder configurations and two modalities, NSFL yields mAP@100 improvements up to +81% on QUEST and +70% on a COCO-derived text-to-image benchmark, and provides an additive +19% average gain on an encoder already fine-tuned for logical retrieval. On NevIR, where absolute accuracies are directly interpretable, NSFL doubles pairwise accuracy -- NevIR's both-correct criterion -- from 0.256 to 0.508. The decomposition is exact and general; the operators built on it are engineering realizations rather than a closed algebra, and we state that boundary precisely. Code is available at https://github.com/vladiaidev-lab/NSFL

items.title: Safe Inference-Time Alignment via Lagrangian Reward Augmentation [ ~ ] [ ◼ ]
items.originalTitle: Safe Inference-Time Alignment via Lagrangian Reward Augmentation
items.summary: arXiv:2607.02781v3 Announce Type: replace Abstract: Inference-time alignment steers a frozen language model during decoding using auxiliary reward signals, avoiding the cost of repeated weight updates. However, existing inference-time alignment methods typically optimize a single scalar score, so explicit safety constraints must either be ignored or encoded through manually tuned penalties. We propose Lagrangian Reward Augmentation (LARA), a general inference-time alignment framework under safety constraints. Starting from a KL-regularized constrained objective with a reward model and a cost model, LARA dualizes the constraint and reduces the optimization problem to a one-dimensional convex problem over a nonnegative dual variable. Estimated on a small calibration set, this dual variable defines an augmented reward that can be used as a drop-in scoring signal within existing inference-time alignment methods. For sequence-level sampling methods, such as Best-of-N reranking, the calibrated dual variable corresponds to the solution of the expected-cost constrained problem. For token-level reward-guided decoding methods, the same construction yields a principled dual-calibrated heuristic rather than an exact constrained-policy guarantee. We evaluate LARA on both sequence-level and token-level inference-time alignment methods, and find that LARA improves the helpfulness-harmlessness tradeoff, with Best-of-N achieving the best performance among inference-time methods, approaching finetuning-based direct alignment baselines.

items.title: Frozen Factor or Spectral Band? In LoRA, the Factor Matters More at Low Rank [ ~ ] [ ◻ ]
items.originalTitle: Frozen Factor or Spectral Band? In LoRA, the Factor Matters More at Low Rank
items.summary: arXiv:2610.06621v2 Announce Type: replace Abstract: On two main task-model pairs, at ranks 1 to 8 with few optimiser steps, the factor a LoRA variant freezes matters more than its band of singular directions. MiCA and PiCa are compared by band, minor against dominant, yet MiCA freezes the output factor B and PiCa, in our notation, the input factor A. We cross factor and band in a 2 x 2 design on models from 1B to 8B parameters. Freezing A beats freezing B on both bands, by +12 to +20 points at rank 2 on a format task, our primary evidence, and still by about +7 points at rank 8 on OpenBookQA. A Holm correction over 258 primary tests, added post hoc, keeps this advantage in 15 of 16 tests and the lead of factor over band at ranks 1, 2 and 4, rank 1 of the format task being itself post hoc. At rank 8 that lead passes its own test but not the correction. The advantage repeats at rank 2 with two 7B models, by +11 to +13 points. Outside the correction, it repeats on GSM8K with a 1B model and, in a post hoc experiment, with an 8B model at ranks 8 and 16. It holds when B frozen gets as many parameters or more, with a random frozen A, and with sixteen times the format-task budget. It narrows above rank 8 on most pairs, at rank 8 with the 8B model on the two main tasks, on ARC and in a task mixture, and it closes at the last step of longer training on OpenBookQA. At MiCA's and PiCa's own settings, it is smaller or not detected.

items.title: Representation Redistribution in Sparse Autoencoders [ ~ ] [ ◻ ]
items.originalTitle: Representation Redistribution in Sparse Autoencoders
items.summary: arXiv:2610.21240v2 Announce Type: replace Abstract: Presenting the same request with different context or formatting can change which sparse autoencoder (SAE) features respond inside a language model. Understanding these changes raises two questions. Which feature responses recur across related inputs, and which of them contribute to downstream computation? We study this phenomenon as representation redistribution and introduce the redistribution sensitivity score (RSS) to identify large feature changes that recur in a consistent direction. We select features on one set of prompt variants and evaluate them on separate variants. Across 27 pretrained SAEs spanning eight language models, RSS reveals a consistent pattern of redistribution. Context and wrapper transformations produce stronger recurring responses than local edits. We then use two frozen safety readouts to measure how these changes contribute to downstream computation. RSS identifies features with approximately twice the mean held out contribution of features selected by the largest readout coefficients, using activation responses alone. An exact decomposition explains how feature changes and readout coefficients determine their effects on the decision margin. Combining RSS contributions with the clean margin improves recurrent failure AUROC from 0.863 to 0.935 and from 0.901 to 0.958, approaching the full readout results of 0.965 and 0.964. These findings show that recurring changes in sparse representations provide a way to identify features with meaningful downstream contributions. Code is available at https://github.com/OpenSAE/Redistribution-Sensitivity-Score.

items.title: Behavioral Compositionality of Sparse Autoencoder Representations [ ~ ] [ ◻ ]
items.originalTitle: Behavioral Compositionality of Sparse Autoencoder Representations
items.summary: arXiv:2610.21261v2 Announce Type: replace Abstract: Sparse autoencoders (SAEs) provide features that can be combined to explain and steer language model behavior. Understanding these combinations requires knowing how reliably individual feature effects predict their joint impact on the model. We study this relationship by retaining or removing subsets of SAE feature contributions and measuring the resulting behavioral responses. We introduce SAE Additivity Residuals (SAR) to quantify how much behavioral variation is explained by feature interactions beyond a chosen order. We prove that, under independent feature subset sampling, SAR measures the normalized energy of these interactions and bounds errors in ranking feature combinations. Across 18 model and behavior settings, learned SAE coordinates have lower first order residuals than matched rotations of the same activation subspace. This shows that SAE coordinates support comparatively simple descriptions of joint feature effects. Pairwise modeling further improves the ranking of held out feature combinations in all 18 settings. We also demonstrate the practical value of modeling these interactions. Across five challenging benchmarks, pairwise models select feature combinations that give higher probability to the correct answer and preserve the original behavioral response more closely than first order models. In MMLU-Pro steering, pairwise modeling improves rank fidelity from 0.5874 to 0.7790 and reduces ordering error from 0.1444 to 0.0606. These results establish behavioral compositionality as a measurable property of SAE representations and show how modeling feature interactions improves the analysis and selection of feature combinations.

items.title: MOZAIC: An Audio-Video Deepfake Benchmark for Telling What Is Fake [ ~ ] [ ◻ ]
items.originalTitle: MOZAIC: An Audio-Video Deepfake Benchmark for Telling What Is Fake
items.summary: arXiv:2611.31301v2 Announce Type: replace Abstract: Audio-video (AV) deepfakes can fake the face, the voice, or both. Most benchmarks only ask whether a clip is real or fake, so they cannot show whether a detector relies on the picture, the voice, or encoding traces. We present MOZAIC, a paired benchmark with a 4-way label in which every source clip is released in all four combinations of real or fake video and real or fake audio so each modality contribution can be measured directly. Fakes cover inner-face swapping, whole-frame video diffusion and voice conversion. MOZAIC has 137,745 clips from 15,014 source pairs and four tasks: T1 AV authenticity, T2 manipulation type, T3 identity verification and T4 explanation. We evaluate 12 AV multimodal LLMs (MLLMs), train four detectors and fine-tune MLLMs with LoRA. Overall, the best MLLM reaches only 35.6% on the four-way T1 and catches far more video-only fakes than voice-only fakes (43.6% vs 7.5%). Trained detectors reach 98.4% on T1, and LoRA fine-tuning raises explanation scores (OmniVinci 4.17 to 7.40, Qwen2.5-Omni 4.42 to 6.98), but the best T1 detector falls to 78.3% when the face-swap generator is held out of training, so generalization and explanation remain open. We release the dataset, the compact MOZAIC-SMALL split, the code and the prompts. https://vectorinstitute.github.io/mozaic/

items.title: GaokaoMathGen: Chinese Gaokao Mathematics Finale Problem Generation Controlled by Latent Reasoning Structures [ ~ ] [ ◻ ]
items.originalTitle: GaokaoMathGen: Chinese Gaokao Mathematics Finale Problem Generation Controlled by Latent Reasoning Structures
items.summary: arXiv:2611.31823v2 Announce Type: replace Abstract: Generating Chinese Gaokao mathematics finale problems requires controlling not only the included skills, but also the underlying mathematical kernel and solution path. Existing LLM-based methods mainly rely on surface-level specifications, while the realized difficulty of generated problems cannot be determined directly from prompted targets. Therefore, we propose GaokaoMathGen, a framework for Chinese Gaokao mathematics finale problem generation controlled by latent reasoning structures. It extracts standardized latent reasoning structures from seed problems and performs constrained synthesis using skills, methods, a core identity, and a pivot step as structural controls. We further estimate realized difficulty through logical-quality filtering, fixed-solver decoding effort, structural features, and solver-output search signals. Experiments show that semantic normalization improves cross-annotator comparability and that 78.0% of 609 scored candidates pass the logical-quality filter. In a teacher audit of the 60 highest-effort candidates, all were judged to reach finale or penultimate problem difficulty, and only one exhibited a severe logical issue. These results support latent reasoning structures as effective control signals for generating high-difficulty mathematical problems.

items.title: How Much Dependency Can a Marginal Rule See? Total Correlation in Diffusion LM Parallel Decoding [ ~ ] [ ◻ ]
items.originalTitle: How Much Dependency Can a Marginal Rule See? Total Correlation in Diffusion LM Parallel Decoding
items.summary: arXiv:2611.31990v1 Announce Type: cross Abstract: A masked diffusion language model is fast because it commits several tokens per step. Each token is sampled from its own marginal, so the dependency between the tokens is lost, and the size of that loss is the conditional total correlation C of the committed set. Most decoders choose the set from per-position marginals, which can bound C but cannot determine it. We ask how well they predict it. We estimate C for fixed candidate sets on four masked diffusion LMs from two families. On three of the four, the best marginal-only predictor is off by about one bit (0.74 to 1.17), 1.8 to 3.7 times less than a baseline that knows only the bound, and most of this accuracy comes from the bound itself. On a subset, our estimate ranks sets like the exact KL cost of a parallel commit, but sits a median 0.4 to 1.1 bits below it on prose and when the rest of the text is still masked. Dream-instruct is the exception, mainly on prose, where its conditionals are least self-consistent. Among six common marginal rules, pooling over the set beats gating on its weakest position in all 24 paired comparisons. The measurement needs a validated readout: Dream and LLaDA place a position's prediction at different logit indices, and the wrong index inflates an inconsistency diagnostic 14 to 41 times. We give three checks that measure the convention. Our results concern predicting C for a fixed set, not what a dependency-aware decoder gains.
